taxonomy.note: Accepted species; Texas native material corresponds to subsp. vomitoria.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Ilex vomitoria and lists Texas in its native range; Texas material belongs to accepted subsp. vomitoria.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes I. vomitoria.
Travis County — Texas Wildbuds documents natural I. vomitoria in Austin/Travis County and describes it as native in central Texas.
Williamson County — the University of Texas Plant Resources Center includes I. vomitoria in the county flora and provides a dedicated detailed treatment.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Purola Preserve lists its own yaupon occurrence as introduced, so that planted Hays-site record is not used. The Hays county decision comes from the independent project native-source list. Landscape cultivars such as 'Nana' and 'Pendula' are not wild-range evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at leaf size and persistence: yaupon is the small-leaved evergreen holly here—tiny leathery elliptic/obovate leaves with low rounded crenate teeth, often on a multi-stemmed pale-gray shrub or small tree.
diagnostic_traits: evergreen multi-stemmed shrub or small tree
leaves alternate, simple, leathery, commonly only 1–4 cm long
leaf blades elliptic to obovate/ovate, usually blunt or rounded at the tip
margins finely crenate/low-toothed, not strongly spiny
bark pale to light gray and often mottled or patched
small white unisexual flowers occur in axillary clusters; plants are dioecious
female plants produce abundant persistent red drupes
native Texas material is Ilex vomitoria subsp. vomitoria

confusers.separator: Possumhaw has larger thin leaves and drops them in winter; yaupon keeps its small leathery foliage year-round.
American holly becomes a larger tree and has much larger thick leaves with conspicuous sharp spine-tipped teeth; yaupon leaves are small with low rounded teeth.

Japanese holly is an introduced landscape shrub with similarly small evergreen leaves but typically black fruit and different leaf/tooth characters; do not use landscape occurrence as native evidence.
